{"id": "21:66/q03", "question": "What does Abraham's question accomplish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q03/p1", "position": "It rebukes idol worship as unreasonable because its objects can neither benefit nor harm.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, al-Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, al-Biqai, al-Bursevi, al-Alusi, Ibn Ashur, al-Tabatabai and Asad describe the rebuke. Al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Ashur and al-Tabatabai stress that their admission made the proof decisive; al-Nasafi calls it an argument. Al-Tabrisi adds that idols capable of help or harm would have defended themselves. Al-Bursevi and al-Alusi say knowing their condition requires giving up worship. Al-Tabatabai says worship seeks good or fears harm; Asad says the people are urged to reason. Ibn Ashur and al-Tabatabai say Abraham turns their admission against them rather than defending himself."}]}
{"id": "21:66/q04", "question": "What is worshipped besides God here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q04/p1", "position": "Their idols, described also as images or statues.", "reasons": "Yahya ibn Sallam identifies the powerless objects as their idols; Ibn Atiyya calls them images and Abu Hayyan statues. The other named sources likewise specify idols when explaining the question."}]}
{"id": "21:66/q05", "question": "Who has the power and right that their objects of worship lack?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q05/p1", "position": "God alone merits worship and controls benefit and harm; mere ability to affect either would not by itself suffice for worship.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi specifies reward for worship and punishment for neglect; Ibn al-Jawzi urges worship of the One who owns benefit and harm. Al-Biqai calls God the supreme sovereign with complete attributes. Al-Qashani says He alone is the beneficial and harmful agent. Al-Tabrisi adds that only the creator of life, desire, power and reason, who can reward and punish, deserves worship; power to benefit or harm alone is insufficient. Ibn Ata, as reported by al-Sulami and al-Bursevi, also names God as controller of harm, benefit and the return."}]}
{"id": "21:66/q06", "question": "In what practical sense can the idols neither benefit nor harm?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q06/p1", "position": "They give no benefit when worshipped and inflict no harm when ignored.", "reasons": "Muqatil and al-Baghawi give the worshipped versus abandoned contrast. Al-Suddi says they neither provide nor give anything and do not harm nonworshippers; al-Kalbi says they do no good when worshipped and no harm when abandoned. Ibn al-Jawzi repeats the giving and abandonment contrast; al-Bursevi says awareness of this should end worship. Al-Nasafi specifically describes the lack of harm to nonworshippers."}]}
{"id": "21:66/q07", "question": "How is 'anything' construed with 'benefit'?", "turns_on": "Whether 'anything' intensifies the negated benefit itself or marks the domain in which no benefit occurs.", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q07/p1", "position": "It is an emphatic verbal noun: they do not benefit you at all.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafi says 'anything' is a verbal noun meaning 'benefit'; al-Alusi offers the equivalent sense that the idols benefit you not at all."}, {"id": "21:66/q07/p2", "position": "It means that they do not benefit you in anything.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this as an alternative construal of the phrase."}]}
{"id": "21:66/q08", "question": "Why is benefit mentioned before harm?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q08/p1", "position": "The order follows what this context foregrounds, especially the worshippers' hoped-for help.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan says harm normally leads because worshippers fear punishment before hoping for reward, whereas benefit leads when foregrounded. It counts seven benefit-first passages, three using nouns and four verbs; it cites 7:188, 6:71, 10:106, 21:66 and 25:55, and explains 7:188 by earlier guidance and good before evil. Its comparison with 13:15 and 34:39 says each passage's order coheres with its own context rather than repeating mechanically. Al-Biqai says the people urgently sought help after their idols were smashed, so anticipated benefit precedes feared harm."}]}
{"id": "21:66/q09", "question": "How does the idols' inability to speak lead into this challenge?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q09/p1", "position": "Their admission that the idols cannot speak exposes their incapacity, enabling Abraham to challenge their worship.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi say the admission made his argument decisive; al-Baydawi says worship contradicted their admission. Al-Burhan links the preceding exchange to this question, and Islahi says the helplessness was already evident (21:65). Ibn Ashur reasons that lack of speech entails no mind, knowledge, will or power, and thus no ability to benefit or harm. Al-Tabatabai says Abraham turned their admission into proof that idols neither know nor act; Kuran Yolu says their own confession exposed the absurdity of their faith. Abu Hayyan says the rebuke follows the proof."}]}
{"id": "21:66/q10", "question": "What wider lesson is drawn about relying on other creatures?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q10/p1", "position": "Seek God rather than help from equally needy creatures or anything besides Him.", "reasons": "Ibn Ata, in al-Sulami and al-Bursevi, says God calls servants to Himself and cuts them off from all else: a powerless creature cannot replace the One who controls benefit, harm and return. Hamdun al-Qassar, in al-Sulami, al-Bursevi and al-Alusi, likens one creature seeking another's help to a prisoner asking another prisoner. Al-Bursevi's spiritual masters say seeking another shows distance from God; all besides Him is play and falsehood, while the Lord suffices. Al-Alusi draws the same warning about needy creatures seeking other needy creatures. Al-Qashani says worship and reverence belong to God alone as the sole agent of benefit and harm."}]}
{"id": "21:66/q11", "question": "What account illustrates reliance on God for provision?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q11/p1", "position": "Habib al-Ajami worshipped God instead of earning wages, and God supplied food and gold after his wife demanded payment.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevi relates that his wife first urged him to earn; he worshipped all night and said he was ashamed to ask the Generous One for pay. After three days she demanded wages or divorce; he returned from another night of worship to find food and a bag of gold sent by God, and she repented."}]}
{"id": "21:66/q12", "question": "How did the idolaters react to Abraham's criticism?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q12/p1", "position": "Bigotry led them to decide to burn him and defend their gods themselves.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu says they could not endure his criticism and protected their gods instead of expecting their gods to protect them."}]}
{"id": "21:66/q13", "question": "How does Abraham's episode fit the sura's sequence of prophets?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q13/p1", "position": "It belongs to a sequence of earlier prophetic guidance that confronts Muhammad's opponents with the fate of past deniers.", "reasons": "Islahi links the section to 21:24's earlier prophets: from verses 48–77 it lists celebrated prophets in ascending order, beginning with Moses and Abraham, whose message matches the Quran's. Moses comes first as the last preceding law-bearing messenger, Aaron assists him, then Abraham and his descendants' two branches appear, followed by Noah. Abraham is founder and leader of the Israelite and Ishmaelite branches, explaining Isaac, Jacob and Lot. The series evokes the whole history of guidance and warns persistent opponents of earlier deniers' fate."}]}
{"id": "21:66/q14", "question": "Where else does the Quran make the point that idols cannot help or harm?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q14/p1", "position": "Several other verses pose comparable questions about powerless idols.", "reasons": "The Study Quran lists 5:76, 6:71, 10:18, 10:106, 13:16, 20:89, 22:12 and 25:55. Al-Burhan also compares 7:188, 6:71, 10:106 and 25:55 when discussing benefit before harm, and 13:15 and 34:39 when discussing contextual word order."}]}
{"id": "21:66/q15", "question": "What does this verse's ending show about the sura's rhyme?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "21:66/q15/p1", "position": "Its ending departs from the sura's usual rhyme because the intended meaning governs the wording.", "reasons": "Al-Samarrai points to 21:66 as an instance of a differing verse ending."}]}
{"id": "21:87/q01", "question": "Who is Dhū al-Nūn?", "turns_on": "The cited interpretations differ in report, language, or doctrinal inference.", "positions": [{"id": "21:87/q01/p1", "position": "Jonah son of Mattā, called the man of the fish or whale.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Ṭabarī identify Jonah son of Mattā; 68:48 calls him the fish's companion. Abū Ḥayyān gives the plural nīnān; al-Ālūsī adds anwān. Al-Qurṭubī records a separate usage of nūna for a child's chin dimple."}, {"id": "21:87/q01/p2", "position": "Inwardly, a spirit not yet perfected.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī's inward reading makes Dhū al-Nūn a spirit short of perfection."}]}

{"id": "21:87/q03", "question": "Was Mattā Jonah's father or mother?", "turns_on": "The cited interpretations differ in report, language, or doctrinal inference.", "positions": [{"id": "21:87/q03/p1", "position": "His father.", "reasons": "Kaʿb names Mattā as father; al-Ālūsī cites Ibn Ḥajar's authentication, gives Hebrew name variants and says no connected genealogy is known."}, {"id": "21:87/q03/p2", "position": "His mother.", "reasons": "Jāmiʿ al-Uṣūl and Ibn al-Athīr say Mattā was the mother; al-Ālūsī reports the exceptional maternal naming claim."}]}
{"id": "21:87/q04", "question": "Did the fish episode precede Jonah's mission to Nineveh?", "turns_on": "The cited interpretations differ in report, language, or doctrinal inference.", "positions": [{"id": "21:87/q04/p1", "position": "Yes: God sent him to Nineveh after he emerged.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says his mission began after emergence. The king assignment narrative also puts the fish before Nineveh."}, {"id": "21:87/q04/p2", "position": "No: he preached before leaving and being swallowed.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says most scholars put the episode after his preaching; al-Wāḥidī prefers this repeated account. 10:98 concerns the people's repentance. Some accounts have him return after rescue."}]}
{"id": "21:87/q05", "question": "Where did Jonah and the fish travel?", "turns_on": "The cited interpretations differ in report, language, or doctrinal inference.", "positions": [{"id": "21:87/q05/p1", "position": "Nineveh was by Mosul on the Tigris; the fish traveled through river and sea.", "reasons": "Yahyā places Nineveh near Mosul on the Tigris and reports Ibn ʿAbbās's river-sea route; al-Thaʿlabī mentions al-Abulla, Ibn Kathīr a fish from the Green Sea."}, {"id": "21:87/q05/p2", "position": "A Jewish account places departure at Jaffa for Tarshish.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports and rejects the Jewish Jaffa–Tarshish flight as unworthy of a prophet."}]}
{"id": "21:87/q06", "question": "What happened when Nineveh repented?", "turns_on": "The cited interpretations differ in report, language, or doctrinal inference.", "positions": [{"id": "21:87/q06/p1", "position": "The people pleaded with children and animals, and punishment was lifted.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Yahyā report public pleading with mothers, children and animals, separation of young, and God lifting promised punishment. Other accounts mention the deadline and Jonah's shame."}, {"id": "21:87/q06/p2", "position": "They repented after Jonah returned from the fish and warned them anew.", "reasons": "Islāḥī and related reports say Jonah was sent back after recovery, preached anew, and the king and people put on sackcloth, fasted and repented."}]}
{"id": "21:87/q07", "question": "Whom was Jonah angry with?", "turns_on": "The cited interpretations differ in report, language, or doctrinal inference.", "positions": [{"id": "21:87/q07/p1", "position": "His people.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and many others say the people denied or later seemed to make him a liar. Islāḥī says the object is contextually implied. Several authors note he left before permission."}, {"id": "21:87/q07/p2", "position": "A king or leading prophet who pressed him.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash reports the king account. Some name Hezekiah and Isaiah or Shuʿyāʾ; Jonah asks whether God had named him. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this remote from other texts."}, {"id": "21:87/q07/p3", "position": "His Lord.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers anger at the Lord from the following supposition and says alleged disobedience of a stay-command would be graver. Al-Rāzī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reject literal anger at God as unfit for prophets."}, {"id": "21:87/q07/p4", "position": "For God's sake, at his people's disobedience.", "reasons": "Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and al-Naḥḥās take lām causally, as in 'angry for you'; al-Naḥḥās compares the Prophet's instruction to ʿĀʾisha. Al-Qurṭubī calls it the best gloss."}, {"id": "21:87/q07/p5", "position": "Himself.", "reasons": "Al-Junayd says Jonah was angry at himself; al-Qushayrī makes this resistance to self and religious opponents."}, {"id": "21:87/q07/p6", "position": "No specified object; he felt affronted by seeming a liar.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says Jonah felt affronted at appearing a liar; he cites a poem equating ghaḍab and anaf and another on resenting an insult. {"id": "21:87/q08", "question": "Why did Jonah depart?", "turns_on": "The cited interpretations differ in report, language, or doctrinal inference.", "positions": [{"id": "21:87/q08/p1", "position": "Persistent rejection exhausted him and he left before permission.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Kashshāf and Islāḥī describe prolonged denial and departure before permission; Islāḥī says a messenger cannot abandon his post at his own judgment."}, {"id": "21:87/q08/p2", "position": "His people were spared and he feared being called a liar.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba cites long abuse and shame when the promised punishment failed to arrive; al-Wāḥidī prefers this post-mission account. Ibn ʿĀshūr disputes the account."}, {"id": "21:87/q08/p5", "position": "He feared execution under a custom of killing liars.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī and others report the custom of killing proven liars; Ibn ʿAṭiyya judges this weak and unsuitable."}, {"id": "21:87/q08/p6", "position": "An urgent mission left no time to prepare.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan reports an urgent command that allowed not even time for sandals; Ibn ʿAbbās has a request for a mount."}, {"id": "21:87/q08/p7", "position": "He believed he had discharged his duty and could migrate.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says Jonah thought God might send another messenger; Islāḥī says he judged his warning sufficient and hoped for relief."}]}
{"id": "21:87/q09", "question": "How does mughāḍiban function?", "turns_on": "The cited interpretations differ in report, language, or doctrinal inference.", "positions": [{"id": "21:87/q09/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial accusative; the form can mean simple or intense anger.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says a reciprocal mufaʿala form can describe one actor, comparing sāfara and nāwala. {"id": "21:87/q10", "question": "How is mughāḍiban read?", "turns_on": "The cited interpretations differ in report, language, or doctrinal inference.", "positions": [{"id": "21:87/q10/p1", "position": "A passive mughḍaban or mughāḍaban.", "reasons": "Abū Sharaf's reported passive form varies with or without alif and in the ḍād vowel; al-Zamakhsharī derives the alifless form from aghḍaba."}, {"id": "21:87/q10/p2", "position": "The common active participle.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives the general active participle."}]}

{"id": "21:87/q14", "question": "What happened to Jonah on the ship and in the fish?", "turns_on": "The cited interpretations differ in report, language, or doctrinal inference.", "positions": [{"id": "21:87/q14/p1", "position": "Lots chose him; he was cast overboard and swallowed unharmed.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī, Ibn Kathīr and others recount a storm, lots, casting overboard, and a whale told to spare flesh and bones because Jonah was prisoner rather than food. {"id": "21:87/q22", "question": "What wrongdoing does Jonah confess?", "turns_on": "The cited interpretations differ in report, language, or doctrinal inference.", "positions": [{"id": "21:87/q22/p1", "position": "Disobedience and sin, repented by confession.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Muḥammad ibn Qays and al-Ḥasan report confession of disobedience and repentance; al-Qushayrī says confession itself seeks pardon."}, {"id": "21:87/q22/p2", "position": "Leaving without permission and failing to persist patiently.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Māwardī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and later authors say Jonah departed without permission; Ibn ʿĀshūr notes kāna and membership among wrongdoers strengthen self-accusation."}, {"id": "21:87/q22/p3", "position": "Desiring punishment and resenting the reprieve.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba and al-Wāḥidī emphasize his wish for punishment and indignation at repentance; al-Qurṭubī reports this and compares Noah's prayer."}, {"id": "21:87/q22/p4", "position": "Human shortcoming before God's majesty.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī emphasizes human fallibility; Bursevī compares the Prophet's statement that he cannot enumerate God's praise."}, {"id": "21:87/q22/p5", "position": "Leaving the better course without intrinsic sin.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Islāḥī say he left a better course or acted with an unintended implication, without intrinsic sin."}, {"id": "21:87/q22/p6", "position": "An inward failure of justice or desire for other than God.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī and al-Ālūsī report inward interpretations of injustice toward lower faculties or a secret desire for other than God."}]}
